justification_text:
My point estimates across the three horizons reflect a broadly stable near-term outlook with only modest drift upward over time. The 1-day estimate of 316.5 is anchored heavily to the prevailing price or index level at the time of the forecast, assuming mean-reversion tendencies dominate over such a short window and that no major scheduled catalysts are imminent. The 1-week estimate of 317.0 nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend momentum, while the 1-month estimate of 318.0 extends that trajectory further but with diminishing conviction about direction. Essentially, the point estimates embody a "random walk with slight upward drift" framework, where the central tendency barely moves but the range of plausible outcomes fans out considerably as the horizon extends.

The confidence interval widths are deliberately calibrated to widen with horizon in a manner consistent with the square-root-of-time scaling common in financial volatility modeling. At 1 day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 8.5 points reflects typical intraday-to-overnight realized volatility. At 1 week, the interval widens to approximately plus or minus 17 points, and at 1 month it expands further to roughly plus or minus 33 points. Key sources of uncertainty include macroeconomic data releases, central bank communication shifts, geopolitical developments, and liquidity conditions, all of which compound over longer windows and make precise forecasting increasingly difficult.

Tail risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden monetary policy surprises — an unexpected rate decision or hawkish pivot in forward guidance — which could easily move markets by more than the stated bounds in a single session. A significant geopolitical shock, a financial contagion event such as a major institutional failure, or an unexpected inflation print far from consensus could all generate moves well beyond the 1-month interval. On the upside, a dramatic improvement in economic sentiment, a ceasefire in an active conflict zone, or a positive earnings or data surprise cascade could similarly breach the upper bound.

It is also worth acknowledging that these intervals assume relatively normal market functioning. If liquidity deteriorates sharply — as it can during periods of stress — realized volatility can spike to multiples of its baseline, rendering even wide confidence intervals too narrow. Additionally, the estimates assume no structural break in the underlying series, an assumption that holds most of the time but fails precisely when it matters most. Forecast users should treat these intervals as reasonable probabilistic guides under baseline conditions rather than hard bounds on possible outcomes.
